correctness.rationale: With the stated no-2pi Fourier convention, the divergence theorem gives i/r times the edge sum. Its uniform O(min(1,1/r)) transform bound gives a positive continuous finite radius for 0<p<2. In the cusp calculation, the nonparallel-edge sum is O(1/r) after factoring out i/r; its angular derivative is O(1), while the parallel-edge sum and derivative are O(1) and O(r). Thus the nonparallel terms change by O(|theta|) against r^(p-3). Opposite parallel edges have distinct support heights. Their unattenuated oscillatory integral is locally C^1 in the nonzero phase frequency by integration by parts; after subtracting its value the attenuation rescales to an L^1 kernel at frequency tending to infinity. Extending that kernel from its moving lower bound to zero introduces a lower-order term, so Riemann–Lebesgue eliminates the cross-edge cusp. The self-edge calculation with beta=2-p uses the triangular sinc-squared kernel and integrates to pi*2^beta/[Gamma(3+beta)sin(pi beta/2)]; rescaling by ell/2 and multiplying by p/A gives the stated additive coefficient. Taylor expansion gives the reciprocal radius, whose exponent below one is incompatible with a Lipschitz polar support function. At p>=2 the nonoscillatory positive sum of squared facet lengths produces a divergent diagonal radial integral at each facet normal; the oscillatory cross and the O(r^-2) Fourier remainder have lower growth order. The conclusion there is unboundedness, not a blanket nonconvexity claim. LMZ Theorem 9 supplies the p<=1 result in the same convention. Frozen VERIFICATION.md and check.py were inspected, not executed; their triangle/square/trapezoid checks are corroborative, not the proof.

value.rationale: The theorem turns the earlier square counterexample into a universal obstruction for polygons and supplies a reusable local invariant: the leading reciprocal-radius defect at any given facet normal is determined by a precise sum of the facet lengths to a specific power. The computation handles unequal opposite edges without assuming symmetry and gives a regularity-based reason for failure of convexity.
